# Ply operating workflow

This skill is the operating route for Ply's current composer surface. It owns
the workflow and the chosen defaults; it does not own content policy — for
what to generate, likeness prompting, local-vs-generated text, official marks,
or safe-region review, follow the `visual-authoring` skill and the consuming
project's own instructions. Ply's tool correctness and the caller's content
choices are separate authorities (ADR-0014); this skill links them, never
copies them.

Run `bun link` once (or use `bun run ply -- ...`) so the examples below run as
`ply ...`. Run them from a directory that owns the inputs you pass; `-p <dir>`
selects the Project. Generated and matted records publish under `out/` in the
working directory — generation is the only network operation and needs a
Vercel AI Gateway key in `.env.local`; everything else is local and offline.

## 1. Create the Project

```bash
ply project init ~/projects/my-poster
```

A Project is self-contained: Layers, retained content bytes, and Render
history live inside it and survive relocation.

## 2. Bring content in — import or generate

Import an existing local image, or generate one. Both become ordinary Layers.

```bash
ply composition create poster --width 1280 --height 720 -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply composition add poster photo --image source.png --resize-to 1280x \
  -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

Generation is one uniform operation — no subject category, no content gate
(ADR-0014). Full-canvas vs isolated output shape is `--intent`; References
(`--ref`, repeatable) are local files in caller order.

```bash
ply generate "a red barn at noon"                      # no --model: nano-2 (tool default)
ply generate "a presenter portrait" --intent isolated  # shape of output, not a matte
ply generate "restyle this room" --ref room.png --ref palette.png
ply generate show <jobId>    # offline inspection of the published record
ply generate list
ply generate review <jobId>  # offline evidence sheet: References, outputs
```

**Defaults as shipped** (the exact contract lives in `ply generate --help` and
README's generation section): omitting `--model` selects **nano-2** — the
tool's general default, and an explicit `--model` always overrides it.
GPT Image 2 quality selection (`--quality low|medium|high`) is qualified for
`gpt-image` only; omitting `--quality` leaves the provider's own default.
A caller-owned workflow may set a different route (for example, the AI
Launchpad workflow selects `--model gpt-image --quality low` for Kenny
headshot/likeness edits using real identity References — that rule lives in
`assets/creator-cutouts/workflow.md` of `kenneth-liao/ai-launchpad-content`,
not here). Never infer a subject to pick a model; the caller names the route.

## The cheap route — two rules

1. **One command per Layer.** `ply composition add` takes every placement,
   transform, region, effect, and text option `ply layer edit` takes, plus
   the stack position, and publishes the Layer in its final state as one
   revision — or nothing, if any option is refused. Do not add a bare Layer
   and then walk it into place with follow-up edits.
2. **Address Layers by name.** Wherever a Layer id is accepted (`layer
   edit`, `layer inspect`, `layer review`), write `<composition>/<use>` —
   `poster/headline`. Never capture a Layer id from output, store it in a
   file, or wrap ply in a script that does; ids still work, but nothing in
   this workflow needs one.

```bash
ply composition add poster headline --text "Ship It" --font Archivo \
  --weight 800 --font-size 120 --color "#ffffff" \
  --anchor center,center --x 640 --y 360 \
  --shadow "0,6,18,#000000aa" -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer edit poster/headline --text "Shipped" -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

## 3. Optionally matte — a separate local pass

`--intent isolated` is a generation request, **not** a matte. When true alpha
is needed, invoke Matting explicitly on any local PNG (never a generated
checkerboard — apparent transparency is not alpha; see visual-authoring):

```bash
ply matte out/generation/<jobId>/outputs/<sha256>.png --id my-cutout
```

Local inference (BiRefNet, weights under `models/`) runs offline with no
billed hop; a source that already carries true alpha is kept as-is with no
inference. The source bytes are never modified. **Inspect the matte result**
on contrasting backgrounds — a successful pass is not automatic acceptance.

## 4. Ingest as Layers — provenance retained

```bash
ply composition add poster cutout --from-matte <matteId> --resize-to x700 \
  --anchor right,bottom --x 1270 --y 720 -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply composition add poster backdrop --from-generation <jobId> \
  --position bottom -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer edit poster/cutout --from-matte <matteId> -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

The ingesting `add` is still the Layer's one command: size, placement, and
stack position ride along with `--from-matte`/`--from-generation`.

Ingested Layers keep the matte's — and a generated source's job — provenance
inside the Project, resolving offline after the external `out/` files are
gone and the Project has moved. `ply generate`/`ply matte` are the only
adoption routes; the legacy library never receives generated content.

## 5. Build Layers in one command, measure, then edit by name

### Stack position — where the new Layer goes

A new use lands on top by default. `--position` takes `top`, `bottom`,
`before:<use>`, or `after:<use>` (paint order: `before` is beneath), so a
bar slips behind an existing word without a `reorder` that re-lists every
use; an unknown use is refused listing the Composition's use names.
`composition import` takes the same option for the imported set, which
stays contiguous and in source order.

```bash
ply composition add poster bar --shape rectangle --size 560x150 \
  --fill "#e11d48" --anchor center,center --x 640 --y 360 \
  --position before:headline -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

### Caller fonts — any local font file stays editable text

`--font-file <path>` takes a local TrueType/OpenType file in place of a
bundled `--font` family, at add and at edit. Its bytes are retained in the
Project like a bundled face, so render, `measure`, replay, relocation, and
cross-Project import never need the original file. Weight and width
validate against the axes the file really contains (a static face accepts
only its own weight), and a non-font file is refused before anything
publishes. Use it for a display face — a pixel wordmark stays a text Layer
you can retype, not a generated image. Licensing is the caller's concern:
keep the licence file beside the font.

```bash
ply composition add poster wordmark --text "ARCADE" \
  --font-file ~/fonts/PressStart2P-Regular.ttf --font-size 64 \
  --color "#ffe27a" --anchor center,top --x 640 --y 40 \
  --shadow "5,5,0,#5a2a1c" -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

### Text controls

Text Layers pick their type look with `--font` and `--font-size`, plus the
text axes `--weight` and `--width` (ply ADR-0021). Ply renders only weights
and widths the bundled font actually contains — never a synthesized one:
Archivo is the bundled variable face (`wght` 100–900, `wdth` 62–125;
omitted controls resolve to its default instance 400/100, which the
revision stores), and IBM Plex Mono is a static 500 face (only weight 500
and its implicit width 100 — or omission — are accepted, and the revision
stores no axis fields). Out-of-range or unsupported values are refused
before anything is published, naming the family and its allowed range.
A `--font` edit keeps the current weight/width when the new font supports
them and is refused — naming the one-command fix — otherwise; explicit
`--weight`/`--width` on the same edit replace the carried values, so a
variable-font Layer switches to a static face in one edit
(`--font "IBM Plex Mono" --weight 500 --width 100`); a weight/width edit
without `--font` validates against the Layer's retained font and requires
`--font` when the retained bytes match no bundled face.

Text Layers also pick their typography with `--tracking` (letter spacing in
em, −0.5 to 1) and `--line-height` (a unitless multiplier of the font size,
0.5 to 3, or `normal`) — ply#187, ADR-0021. Both are font-independent and
stored only when set: an omitted control paints as normal spacing and the
font's own line height, and `tracking` 0 is the same look as absent, so it
is never stored. Out-of-range or non-numeric values are refused before
anything is published, naming the control and its allowed range (a usage
error). On edit, `--tracking 0` removes stored tracking and `--line-height
normal` removes stored line height; an omitted control keeps its current
value across any edit, including `--font`.

`measure` is read-only, free, and uses the exact font bytes and geometry
rendering uses (a variable-font text Layer's report includes its stored
weight and width, and its stored tracking and line height when set):

```bash
ply composition measure poster -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply composition measure poster headline --json -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

It reports the layout **content box**, the transformed **box**, and the
**painted** extents (visible ink — transparent image padding and loose text
line-boxes are excluded), plus the on-canvas footprint and `clipped`. Effects
and transforms are included: painted bounds grow with the shadow/outline and
follow the rotation. Use it to place and align against numbers, and to check
what a transform will do to the footprint before running it.

Edits are for iteration after the one-command add. They are
non-destructive — placement changes, never retained pixels — and absolute
setters unless noted, so repeating one during iteration is safe. The
exception is `--resize`, which multiplies the current scale and compounds
when repeated: **prefer `--scale`** (absolute, idempotent; image, text,
and shape Layers; mutually exclusive with `--resize`/`--resize-to`).

```bash
ply layer edit poster/headline --scale 1.5 -p ~/projects/my-poster   # absolute: run it twice, same result
ply layer edit poster/headline --resize 1.5 -p ~/projects/my-poster  # relative: scale × 1.5 — compounds
ply layer edit poster/photo --resize-to 800x -p ~/projects/my-poster # image/shape only, aspect preserved
ply layer edit poster/headline --rotate -8 -p ~/projects/my-poster   # absolute angle; 0 removes
ply layer edit poster/photo --flip horizontal -p ~/projects/my-poster  # absolute; none removes
ply layer edit poster/headline --anchor center,center --x 640 --y 360 -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer edit poster/headline --shadow "0,6,18,#000000aa" -p ~/projects/my-poster  # dx,dy,blur,color
ply layer edit poster/headline --outline "2,#101014" -p ~/projects/my-poster        # width,color
ply layer edit poster/headline --weight 800 --width 122 -p ~/projects/my-poster     # text axes (variable fonts only)
ply layer edit poster/headline --tracking -0.032 --line-height 0.88 -p ~/projects/my-poster  # 0/normal removes
ply layer edit poster/headline --opacity 0.9 -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer inspect poster/headline -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

Route rules worth internalizing — a working summary only: the exact setters,
combination restrictions, and exit-code semantics are owned by `ply layer
--help` and README's Layer sections, not restated normatively here.

- **Transform order** is fixed: flip, then scale, then rotation, applied
  about the `(x, y)` placement point; effects paint in the Layer's local
  space and transform with it (an outline is painted before the shadow cast
  from it).
- **`--anchor` targets painted ink, not the top-left corner** — transparent
  padding does not count and glyph ink centers, so the resolution runs
  against the Layer's current transforms. On a one-command `add` the order
  is fixed for you — content, transforms, visible region, anchor, then
  effects — so `--anchor` combines freely with `--shadow`/`--outline`
  there, and the anchor resolves the ink *before* the effects grow it (an
  outline of width w paints w px outside the anchored edge). On `layer
  edit`, `--anchor` cannot combine with `--shadow`/`--outline` in one edit
  (see `ply layer edit --help`, the owner of these restrictions):
  transforms and content first, then anchor, then effects — and re-anchor
  when the geometry later changes.
- **Sharing is explicit:** a Layer referenced by several Compositions
  refuses a bare edit and names the blast radius — choose `--in-place`
  (propagates everywhere) or `--fork` (isolates the named use) deliberately;
  single-referrer edits just apply. A name address does not change this —
  with `--fork` it supplies the Composition and use, so
  `ply layer edit poster/headline --fork ...` needs no `--composition`/`--use`.
- Failures never mutate live state, so a wrong edit is always cheap to retry.

## Shapes, visible regions, and vectors

Three parameter-built capabilities cover the common building blocks without
leaving ply (spec #207): shape Layers for bars, pills, cards, and
backgrounds; the visible region for framing content without touching the
file; and vector import with a paint-time colour for single-colour marks.
All are absolute setters, publish Layer revision facts, and replay
byte-identically after later edits and Project relocation.

### Shape Layers — bars, pills, cards, backgrounds

A shape Layer is created from parameters alone — no image file is read and
no image bytes are stored; its content IS its parameters. `--size` is in
canvas px and `--fill` takes ONE solid colour or ONE gradient:

```bash
# A highlight bar and a rounded pill — nothing to draw in advance:
ply composition add poster strip --shape rectangle --size 830x110 \
  --fill "#ffe27a" --x 140 --y 20 -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply composition add poster pill --shape rectangle --size 220x44 \
  --corner-radius 22 --fill "#22c55ecc" --x 40 --y 650 -p ~/projects/my-poster
# A full-canvas background is an ordinary shape Layer sized to the canvas —
# here a radial teal gradient from the centre out to the farthest side:
ply composition add poster bg --shape rectangle --size 1280x720 \
  --fill "radial:#2a6e69,#123b3a" --position bottom -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

Gradient grammar: `linear:<angle>deg,<stop>,<stop>` (degrees clockwise from
bottom-to-top, the CSS convention) and `radial:<stop>,<stop>`; a stop is
`<color>` or `<color>:<position>` (0–100 percent, the `%` optional), and
stop colours take alpha. Every shape parameter is an absolute setter on
`layer edit` — refit the bar to a new headline instead of remaking it:

```bash
ply layer edit poster/strip --size 560x110 --fill "#e11d48" -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer edit poster/strip --corner-radius 24 -p ~/projects/my-poster   # 0 removes
ply layer edit poster/strip --fill "linear:90deg,#1d4ed8,#22c55e" -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

Placement, transforms, anchored placement, shadow, and outline work on
shape Layers as on any other kind. A radius over half the shorter side is
refused, never clamped; a Layer's kind is stable across edits.

### Visible region — frame content without editing the file

Any Layer — image, text, or shape — can show only a rectangle of its
content, specified in the Layer's OWN content pixels, with an optional
corner radius:

```bash
ply layer edit poster/photo --visible-region "120,80,640,360" -p ~/projects/my-poster  # frame the subject
ply layer edit poster/photo --visible-region-radius 12 -p ~/projects/my-poster         # round the crop's corners
ply layer edit poster/photo --visible-region none -p ~/projects/my-poster              # remove — restores the prior render byte-for-byte
```

Content outside the region is not ink: painted extents, anchored placement,
clipping, and the measurement capture window all follow it, and shadow and
outline hug the cropped edge. That is the route for framing a face from a
wide padded cutout or rounding a screenshot's corners. One-command `add`
takes the region too, and `--anchor` then resolves the cropped ink:

```bash
ply composition add poster face --image wide-cutout.png \
  --visible-region "620,40,640,640" --anchor center,center \
  --x 640 --y 360 -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

### Vector import and vector colour

`--image` accepts a local SVG file at add and at edit: the bytes are
retained unchanged, the Layer records `format: "svg"`, and rendering
re-rasterizes the vector at the painted size and supersample factor — one
file is crisp at 60 px and at 600 px, with no `rsvg-convert` step. An
imported vector is inert: a file referencing anything outside itself is
refused at import (the fix is embedding the resource as a data URI), and a
script in the file never runs. A single-colour mark takes its colour as a
parameter, so one logo file serves dark, light, and brand uses:

```bash
ply composition add poster logo --image ~/brand/logo.svg \
  --vector-color "#e11d48" -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer edit poster/logo --vector-color none -p ~/projects/my-poster  # back to the authored colours
```

`--vector-color` paints over the vector's own alpha — a multi-colour vector
becomes a single-colour silhouette — and is refused on raster image, text,
and shape Layers, which take their colour from retained pixels, `--color`,
and `--fill` respectively.

The exact setters, refusal texts, and numeric bounds are owned by `ply
layer edit --help`, README's shape/visible-region/vector sections, and
`docs/guide/limits.md` — this section is the route, not the contract.

## Look parameters: grade, edge glow, blend modes, and gradient text

Look parameters adjust a Layer's tonal and colour balance, blend interaction,
and lighting feel at paint time without editing source files or calling external
models (spec #218, ADR-0024). They apply uniformly across image (raster and
vector), text, and shape Layers. All look parameters are absolute setters that
publish immutable Layer revision facts, stored only when set; documented neutral
values remove the stored facts.

### Layer grading — brightness, contrast, saturation, and warmth

Grading tunes a Layer's tonal and colour balance so cutouts, shapes, and text sit
naturally in their scene:

- `--brightness <num>`: `0` to `5` (neutral `1`). Values `< 1` darken; `> 1` brighten.
- `--contrast <num>`: `0` to `5` (neutral `1`). Values `< 1` reduce contrast; `> 1` increase it.
- `--saturation <num>`: `0` to `5` (neutral `1`). Values `< 1` desaturate (`0` is greyscale); `> 1` oversaturate.
- `--warmth <num>`: `-1` to `1` (neutral `0`). Positive values shift toward orange/red; negative toward blue.

Every control is an absolute setter applied at paint time to the Layer's content
only — outline, shadow, and alpha coverage are strictly preserved. Setting a
neutral value (`1` for brightness/contrast/saturation, `0` for warmth) removes
that control from the stored revision; when all controls are neutral, the grade
fact is dropped completely:

```bash
# Grade a photo to match a warm studio setting:
ply layer edit poster/photo --brightness 1.15 --contrast 1.1 --saturation 1.1 --warmth 0.25 -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Remove warmth while keeping brightness, contrast, and saturation:
ply layer edit poster/photo --warmth 0 -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Remove all grading, restoring the exact ungraded paint:
ply layer edit poster/photo --brightness 1 --contrast 1 --saturation 1 -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

One-command `add` takes grading controls too:

```bash
ply composition add poster badge --shape rectangle --size 120x40 --fill "#e11d48" \
  --brightness 1.1 --contrast 1.05 --x 50 --y 50 -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

### Edge glow — 2D rim light on the alpha edge

`--glow "<width>,<softness>,<color>[,<angle>,<strength>]"` paints an inner rim of
light just inside the Layer's alpha edge, over the graded content (`none` removes it).
It gives cutouts and shapes a directional rim light matching the scene's light:

- `width` and `softness`: px reach and feather (`0` to `256`).
- `color`: hex color (`#RGB`, `#RRGGBB`, `#RRGGBBAA`).
- `angle` and `strength`: optional direction pair — angle in degrees clockwise
  from top (`-360` to `360`) and strength `0` to `1` (e.g. angle `90` is light
  from the right, angle `0` from the top, angle `270` from the left). Without
  the pair the glow is even all round; strength `0` drops the direction.

```bash
# Rim-light a cutout with warm light coming from the right:
ply layer edit poster/photo --glow "16,8,#ffaa33,75,0.75" -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Switch to an even neon cyan rim light:
ply layer edit poster/photo --glow "12,4,#00e5ff" -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Remove the edge glow:
ply layer edit poster/photo --glow none -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

**The grading-versus-relighting boundary:** Edge glow is a two-dimensional edge
effect on the Layer's own alpha edge. It follows the visible region (including
rounded corners), transforms with the Layer, and never alters alpha coverage or
extends painted extents. It is NOT relighting: changing the direction or shape of
light on a subject, casting shadows across 3D features, or estimating surface
normals is generation (OOS-001, ISC-39), not a Layer parameter.

### Blend modes — composite against the backdrop

`--blend <mode>` sets how the whole Layer composites against everything beneath
it (`normal` removes the stored fact). Allowed modes: `normal`, `multiply`,
`screen`, `overlay`, `soft-light`, `darken`, `lighten`, `color-dodge`.

The whole Layer — content, visible region, grade, edge glow, outline, shadow,
and opacity — blends as ONE unit against the canvas backdrop (ADR-0024):

```bash
# Place a white-background graphic with multiply instead of running a matting pass:
ply composition add poster icon --image white-bg-logo.png --blend multiply \
  --resize-to 200x --x 100 --y 100 -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Screen blend for dark-background lighting elements:
ply layer edit poster/icon --blend screen -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Restore standard compositing:
ply layer edit poster/icon --blend normal -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

### Gradient fill on text

Text Layers share the unified fill grammar through `--color` (#222, spec #218 US-004):
passing `linear:<angle>deg,<stop>,<stop>` or `radial:<stop>,<stop>` renders gradient
text that remains editable text. The gradient automatically spans the glyph ink box
and clips to glyph alpha, while outlines and shadows continue to hug the glyphs:

```bash
ply layer edit poster/headline --color "linear:90deg,#ff5500,#ffaa00" -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer edit poster/headline --color "#ffffff" -p ~/projects/my-poster  # restore solid colour
```

### Look parameters and shared Layers — forks vs in-place

Look parameters are Layer revision facts, shared with the Layer. A different look
for the same shared content is a fork:

- A Layer referenced by multiple Compositions refuses a bare look edit (exit 1)
  and reports the referring Compositions.
- Pass `--fork` to isolate the look changes to the current Composition, minting a
  new Layer identity for that use.
- Pass `--in-place` when the intention is to update the look across all referring
  Compositions simultaneously.

```bash
# Fork the headline look for an alternate composition:
ply layer edit alt-poster/headline --fork --warmth 0.3 --glow "10,4,#38bdf8" -p ~/projects/my-poster

# Update the shared look across every composition:
ply layer edit poster/headline --in-place --contrast 1.2 -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

## 6. Render and review pixels

```bash
ply composition render poster -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

Renders supersample by default (ply ADR-0022): the Composition is painted
at 2 device pixels per canvas pixel, then area-averaged back to exactly the
canvas size — large display type gets even edge ramps instead of
stair-stepping. Composition geometry stays in canvas pixels. Override with
`--supersample <n>` (integer ≥ 1); `--supersample 1` paints directly at the
canvas size (byte-identical to pre-supersampling renders). The render pixel
limits apply to the supersampled paint, so a canvas that fits at 1× but not
at 2× is refused by default and names the fix — the bounds and the workable
canvas/factor table are in `kenneth-liao/ply`'s `docs/guide/limits.md`.

```bash
ply composition render poster --supersample 4 -p ~/projects/my-poster  # smoother
ply composition render poster --supersample 1 -p ~/projects/my-poster  # direct paint
```

Every render writes a manifest recording the supersample factor under the
Project's `renders/`; open the PNG and look at it. Then replay any retained
render byte-identically at its recorded factor — `replay` takes no
`--supersample` flag; the factor comes from the manifest — even after later
edits or relocation:

```bash
ply composition replay <project>/renders/<render-id>.manifest.json -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply layer review poster/cutout --out review.html -p ~/projects/my-poster  # offline evidence sheet
```

### Comparison sheet — review candidates inside ply

`ply composition sheet` lays an ordered list of inputs out as ONE labelled
PNG grid you can open and read directly — no ImageMagick `montage`. Each
input is a Composition name (rendered current), a retained Render manifest,
or a local image file (an existing file wins over a Composition of the same
name). Labels default to the input's name; `--label <1-based index>=<text>`
overrides one. `--columns` (default 2) and `--cell` (default 512, square)
size the grid, and mixed aspect ratios are fitted without distortion.
`--pair` lays the list out as reference-beside-result rows — an even
number of inputs, each reference immediately before its result.

```bash
ply composition sheet poster poster-alt poster-dark --columns 3 \
  --out candidates.png -p ~/projects/my-poster
ply composition sheet reference.jpg poster --pair \
  --label 1="reference" --label 2="ours" --out compare.png -p ~/projects/my-poster
```

The sheet is a review artifact, not a Render: it writes no manifest and
adds nothing to Render history, and without `--out` it lands under the
Project's `guidelines/`. Open it and look.

One raster bound to know: Chromium caps a single outline-dilate kernel at
256 raster pixels. Outline width is in the Layer's local pixels (input
bound 0–256), painted before the transform, so the visible ring is
width × Layer scale and the raster dilation is
width × max(|scaleX|, |scaleY|) × supersample. Over the cap the ring is
drawn as chained dilate steps (n = ceil(dilation / 256)) — never refused —
but each step is a full morphology pass, so a very wide ring can paint
slowly or hit the screenshot timeout (the measured figures and the timeout
live in `kenneth-liao/ply`'s `docs/guide/limits.md`). When a huge ring is
slow, use a thinner outline, a smaller Layer scale, or `--supersample 1`.

## Why visual review remains necessary

Measurement is geometry, and geometry is not layout taste. `measure` tells
you where ink is, whether it clips, and what a transform will do — it does
not tell you whether the composition looks right. It cannot judge balance,
contrast, overlapping legibility, or whether a subject's edge survived the
matte, and it deliberately promises no automatic aesthetic layout: placement
anchors center ink, not attention. Likewise, generation and Matting are
operations, not verdicts — a successful Job is not a good image and a
successful matte is not an approved likeness. Inspect rendered output at the
intended viewing size, compare candidates against their References via
`generate review`/`layer review`, and follow the consuming project's approval
practice (see visual-authoring) before anything is used.

## Contract boundaries

- Command contracts and their full semantics are documented in `README.md`
  (one section per surface) and `docs/project-storage-contract.md`,
  `docs/generation-publication-contract.md`, and
  `docs/matting-publication-contract.md`. This skill teaches the route and
  the defaults; those documents own the exact contracts — do not duplicate
  them here.
- Size, quality, and refusal limits live in `kenneth-liao/ply`'s
  `docs/guide/limits.md` (the ply user guide): the canvas-vs-supersample
  pixel bounds and workable canvas/factor table, the outline width bound
  and chained-dilate cost, `measure`'s ≤1 px tolerances and capture bound,
  the font weight/width refusal and one-edit static-face route, caller-font
  formats and refusals, the vector intrinsic-size and external-reference
  rules, the shape parameter bounds, the comparison sheet's size and input
  limits, and exit-code semantics. Check it before choosing a canvas, supersample
  factor, outline, font edit, shape radius, or vector import.
- Retained history, sharing/fork semantics, relocation, and offline replay
  are governed by ADR-0013; Layer transform/effect canonicalization by
  ADR-0016–0019; visible region by ADR-0023; Layer grade, look paint order,
  and blend mode by ADR-0024. The legacy Scene/library/jobs surface still works unchanged
  and is documented in `README.md`; prefer the composer surface for new work.
- The complete YouTube package workflow (safe regions, channel packaging) is
  a separate caller workflow — the `visual-authoring` skill covers its
  authoring practices; caller instructions own the rest.
